title: Listening in Kalyan
hook: a bee that keeps coming back, a bird that waits for one drop: reading along with a short hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Kalyan, the evening raga that opens with we are your children. Your line was peaceful evening. When the lamps came on, what did the house sound like? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

A bumblebee on a lavender bush doesn't land once and leave. It goes, it circles, it comes back to the same flower. Again, and again. Nobody has to persuade it. Something there is sweet enough. Kalyan, the evening raga we opened yesterday, holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and one of Guru Arjan's hymns there is built around that bee. It's short enough to read along with from start to finish. So today we do exactly that, slowly, line by line.
screen: `A BEE THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.` → `TWO GURUS IN KALYAN.` → `A HYMN SHORT ENOUGH TO READ ALONG.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens with its center line, the one marked Rahao, pause. In paraphrase: grant me this grace, that like the bee drawn to the nectar of the lotus, my mind is drawn to your lotus feet, again and again. In Gurmukhi, again and again is fer fer, and you can hear it turning back on itself. That's the whole prayer of the hymn: not one visit, but a mind that keeps returning. The first verse brings in a second creature, a bird. It's the chatrik, the rainbird we met among Malar's rain pictures, which tradition says drinks only drops of rain. In paraphrase, the hymn says: I have no business with any other water; give this rainbird the drop of the Lord. The second verse closes it. Without meeting, there is no contentment. Seeing the vision, Nanak lives. Guru Arjan signs the hymn with the name Nanak. Now read it again with Kalyan's evening around it. Yesterday, peace looked like a child who knows someone is watching the door. Today the hymn adds something. The bee isn't calm because it stopped moving. It's calm because it knows where it's going back to. The rainbird isn't calm because it's full. It's calm because it knows which drop it's waiting for. Contentment here, santokh, isn't having everything. It's being turned toward one thing. That's a kind of peace an evening can hold: not an empty room, but a mind that has found its flower and keeps landing there. That's why today's practice is to read along once: when you hear Kalyan sung, you'll know where the bee is. Today's line: evening peace.
screen: `RAHAO: DRAWN AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THE RAINBIRD WANTS ONE DROP.` · `NO CONTENTMENT WITHOUT MEETING.` · `PEACE IS BEING TURNED TOWARD ONE THING.` · then, large: `EVENING PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read along once, and then come back again and again. If you can, find this hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan with a translation beside it, and read it once, slowly, while it's sung or in silence. Then sit. Choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nostrils, or, if you pray, the word Waheguru. The mind will wander. That's fine. The bee wanders too. Each time you notice, come back to the same place, gently, without scolding. Count nothing. Just keep landing. The bell holds the time.
Listening in Kalyan. Reading along with Guru Arjan's short hymn: the bee drawn to the lotus again and again, and the rainbird asking for one drop. Today's word.

Your line: evening peace. Tonight, pick one small thing to come back to, a breath, a word, a cup of tea held in both hands, and come back to it three times before bed. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs often read a shabad with a translation open while it is sung in kirtan; some gurdwaras project the Gurmukhi and an English rendering on a screen so the congregation can follow line by line.

what it means: in Guru Arjan's hymn the mind keeps returning to the lotus, like a bee, again and again.
what a scholar hears: the Rahao line carries the hymn's center, and the second verse ties contentment, santokh, to meeting.
